strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated failure mode (functional entanglement) in LLM-driven NAS and proposes a simple, well-specified operator (factor selection + factor-conditioned patching + feasibility enforcement) that directly targets it. Algorithms 1 and 2 are precise enough to reimplement.

The primary comparison is controlled: OpenEvolve vs. SPARK share the same evolutionary backbone, LLM (DeepSeek-R1), and 100-attempt budget, which makes the attribution of gains to the editing operator reasonably clean.

The ablation in Table 2 (ASR only vs. RC+SAR only vs. full SPARK, under two different LLMs) is informative and shows a consistent qualitative trend, suggesting the effect is not specific to one editor model.

The analysis of search dynamics (entanglement rate, cumulative valid rate, best-so-far progress in Fig. 2) connects the mechanism to the outcome rather than only reporting end results, and the appendix includes multi-seed trajectories and full evolved programs, which aids transparency.
Budget accounting between proposal attempts and evaluated candidates is explicitly discussed (Sec. 4), a detail often glossed over in this literature.
weaknesses: Narrow evaluation scope: evolution is performed on a single task (CLRS-DFS) of a single benchmark family, and the factorization is limited to exactly two factors (OPERATOR/ACTION). There is no evidence the method generalizes to other NAS domains (e.g., the image-classifier setting of EvoPrompting), other factorizations, or more than two factors, despite the general framing.

The headline 28.1x sample-efficiency claim is computed against EvoPrompting's best DFS result under a 1600-evaluation setting, i.e., a different protocol (EvoPrompting evolves across multiple tasks; SPARK evolves only on DFS). Comparing across settings inflates the speedup figure; a like-for-like comparison with the re-run baselines would be much less dramatic. Similarly, cross-task results vs. EvoPrompting are confounded by the differing search protocols.

Transfer results are mixed and weaken the aggregate claims: the evolved architecture regresses substantially on several tasks (BFS 99.7->70.6, FW 48.5->32.9, KMP 19.5->14.9, MKr 89.8->86.2), and the headline QS improvement (0.47->10.69) is still nearly a failure. Only 12/18 tasks improve over the CLRS reference and 10/18 over EvoPrompting, yet the abstract and conclusion emphasize the strong average gains without discussing these regressions.

Statistical rigor of the main results is unclear: Table 1 does not state how many seeds underlie the main comparison (the multi-seed analysis in Fig. A.1 covers search dynamics only), and no variance or significance testing is reported for the Table 1/Table 2 numbers, which are single-trajectory search results on a stochastic process.

Citation integrity concerns: the reference list contains multiple apparently irrelevant works cited to support unrelated claims (e.g., Fu et al. on steel-sheet defect recognition for algorithmic alignment, person re-identification and mobile GUI papers cited for message-passing claims), plus future-dated entries (arXiv:2603.05869, '2026'; DeepSeek accessed 2026-01-21) that could not exist as written. This pattern suggests citation padding or unverified references and must be corrected.

The factor regions are hand-annotated boundary tags on the specific CLRS program structure; the paper does not discuss how sensitive results are to how the two regions are drawn, or what happens when a beneficial edit genuinely requires changing both factors (co-design cases that the method forbids by construction).

The term 'progressive knowledge activation' in the title is not clearly operationalized in the method: ASR/RC/SAR are three sequential LLM calls with fixed roles; no progressive or curriculum-like mechanism is demonstrated, making the framing somewhat overclaimed.

No explicit code-release commitment or reproducibility statement for the SPARK implementation and prompts; given the heavy dependence on prompt engineering details (role prompts, tag format, feasibility checks), this limits reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets a real and interesting failure mode in LLM-driven NAS: unconstrained code edits coupling multiple functional decisions ('functional entanglement'), and the proposed remedy (factor tokens, region tags, and factor-local feasibility checks) is a concrete, implementable mechanism.

The controlled comparison against OpenEvolve under an identical search backbone and LLM editor is methodologically sensible, and the two-LLM ablation (DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus) in Table 2 supports that the factorization, not the model choice, drives the gain.
Search dynamics analysis (entanglement rate, cumulative valid rate, best-so-far progress in Fig. 2) goes beyond aggregate accuracy and gives mechanistic evidence for why constrained edits help.

The method is backbone-agnostic and cheap (feasibility checks are far cheaper than full training), and the evolved architectures retain near-reference MACs, ruling out capacity scaling as the source of gains.
weaknesses: Serious citation-integrity problems: the reference list and appendix narrative contain numerous citations that are clearly irrelevant to the claims they support, e.g., 'structural and contextual conditions (Liu et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019)' where Fu et al. 2019 is about steel-sheet surface defects; 'mobile GUI: From pixel-words to screen-sentences' (Fu et al., 2024), 'unsupervised person re-identification' (Li et al., 2024), 'single-image cloud removal' (Wu et al., 2024), 'room expert guided image-goal navigation' (Li et al., 2025a) cited as evidence that SPARK prevents cross-factor entanglement, and a 'camera-aware label refinement' paper (Li et al., 2024) cited for iteration-level message computation. Several of these (e.g., arXiv:2603.05869, 'Qi et al., 2026') appear fabricated or at minimum stuffed in to lend false support to the results. This is a disqualifying integrity concern.

Selective and inconsistent reporting of results: Table 1 reports only a 10-task subset where 'Ours' wins, while Table A.1 (all tasks) shows substantial regressions (BFS 70.6 vs. 99.7 reference and 100.0 for EP; FW 32.9 vs. 48.5/61.4; KMP 14.9 vs. 19.5/16.3; MCO 87.3 vs. 91.7). The claim that SPARK 'achieves the best OOD accuracy across all listed tasks' and the 12/18 (or 10/30) wins are not adequately reconciled with the cherry-picked main table; the abstract's framing does not convey the full picture.

The headline 28.1x 'sample-efficient speedup' compares 57 evaluated candidates against EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation setting, but EvoPrompting evolves across multiple tasks while SPARK evolves only on DFS and transfers. The comparison regimes are not equivalent, so the speedup claim is not a like-for-like measurement.

The headline OOD gains come from a single search run on DFS with per-task evaluation thereafter; multi-seed evidence (Fig. A.1) covers only the 100-attempt DFS trajectory, and error bars/seed variance for the per-task numbers in Table 1 are not reported, which is problematic given CLRS training noise (e.g., QS differences of ~1 point).

Novelty is modest: the core mechanism is prompt-level region tagging plus post-hoc diff-based rejection of edits outside the tagged region. Similar structure-aware constraints exist in grammar-constrained generation and in classical structure-aware NAS mutation operators, as the paper itself notes; the marginal contribution over 'constrain the LLM to edit one region and check the diff' is limited, and no comparison to a simpler baseline (e.g., unconstrained editing with the same feasibility checks but without factor routing) cleanly isolates the routing component's value beyond Table 2's coarse ablation.

Presentation issues: duplicated reference entries (Zoph & Le 2017a/b), inconsistent numbers between main text and appendix (DFS CLRS 46.78 vs. 47.8; EP 68.14 vs. 68.1; '12/18 tasks' vs. the 30-task appendix table), and heavy quotation-mark-laden terminology ('Searching: Function→Patch', 'Factor A or B') that obscures rather than clarifies the method.

No code or implementation details sufficient for reproduction (region tag definitions, prompts, and the exact entanglement criterion are deferred to an 'Appendix' that does not actually contain them in the provided material), undermining the reproducibility of the central claims.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: the paper identifies 'functional entanglement' (one free-form edit coupling Operator- and Action-level changes) as a concrete, plausible failure mode of LLM-driven NAS, which is a more specific diagnosis than generic 'LLMs are noisy optimizers' narratives.

Well-designed controlled comparison: SPARK and OpenEvolve share the same evolutionary backbone, the same LLM (DeepSeek-R1-0528), the same 100-attempt budget, and the same CLRS harness, so the accuracy/validity differences are attributable to the editing operator itself.

Useful ablation design: Table 2 separates scope selection (ASR) from scope-local refinement (RC+SAR) under two different LLM editors (DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus) with consistent qualitative trends, supporting that the mechanism—not a particular model—drives gains.

Compute attribution is handled carefully: MACs are reported alongside accuracy, the best-so-far MAC trajectory (Fig. A.1b) shows no systematic compute inflation, and budget accounting distinguishes proposal attempts from evaluated candidates.

Reliability analysis goes beyond aggregate accuracy: entanglement rate and cumulative valid rate (Fig. 2b–c) are measured over the trajectory, and the appendix provides multi-seed dynamics and full program evolution traces (Listings 1–6), aiding reproducibility of the qualitative story.
weaknesses: The headline '28.1× sample-efficient speedup' is an apples-to-oranges comparison: it divides EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation budget (its original paper setting) by the 57 evaluated candidates in the authors' own pipeline, while the EvoPrompting number in Table 1 (68.14 OOD on DFS) appears to come from a different protocol than the rerun OpenEvolve/FunSearch/EoH baselines. A controlled speedup claim against baselines under identical accounting is never actually established.

Serious citation-integrity concerns: the reference list contains multiple clearly irrelevant works (steel-surface defect recognition, unsupervised person re-ID, mobile GUI understanding, cloud removal, homography estimation), and these are cited in the appendix to support unrelated technical claims (e.g., Fu et al. 2019 for residual shortcut signals, Qi et al. 2026 for masking). This pattern of citation padding undermines confidence in the manuscript's overall rigor.

Inconsistent evaluation scope: the abstract/intro report results on '10 CLRS tasks,' the conclusion claims '12/18 tasks' improvements and 'outperforms EvoPrompting on 10/18,' while the appendix (Table A.1) reports 30 tasks. These numbers do not reconcile, and the appendix reveals regressions on several tasks (e.g., BFS 70.6 vs 99.7 reference, FW 32.9 vs 48.5, KMP 14.9 vs 19.5) that the 10-task main table selection obscures.

Generalization of the core method is asserted but not tested: the factorization S = {OPERATOR, ACTION} is hardcoded to two disjoint code regions of the specific CLRS program structure and requires human annotation of boundary tags. Claims of backbone-agnosticism and applicability beyond CLRS are unsupported; only one benchmark and a single search task (DFS) with transfer are evaluated.

The central mechanism is partly enforced by construction: SPARK's feasibility check rejects any non-factor-local edit, so the lower entanglement rate (Fig. 2b) is largely a direct consequence of the constraint rather than an emergent property; the paper's narrative partly presents an enforced invariant as an empirical finding, though the ablations do partially mitigate this.

No explicit code release or limitations section; results depend on a proprietary LLM API (DeepSeek-R1-0528), and given known prompt-sensitivity of LLM-driven evolution, external reproducibility is uncertain. Multi-seed evidence exists only in the appendix and only for SPARK's own dynamics, not for baseline variance.

Presentation is heavily branded (ASR, RC, SAR, Function-factor Tokens, 'Searching: Function→Patch') for what is, mechanically, a role-decomposed prompting scheme with region-tag constraints and diff-based validation; the terminology inflates the conceptual contribution relative to its simplicity.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear, well-motivated failure mode ('functional entanglement' of holistic LLM edits) and proposes a simple, implementable remedy: factor-scoped editing with explicit region tags and feasibility checks, decomposed into scope selection (ASR) and factor-conditioned refinement (RC+SAR).

The evaluation design is careful in several respects: a controlled comparison against OpenEvolve under an identical backbone and identical LLM editor isolates the contribution of the editing operator; the full 30-task CLRS comparison in Appendix A.1 guards against task-selection bias; and MACs are tracked to show gains are not explained by capacity scaling.

The ablations are unusually thorough for this line of work: Table 3 (ASR vs. RC+SAR under two LLM editors), Table A.2 (scope-control baselines showing region tags alone, fixed scopes, and random scopes are insufficient), and the search-dynamics analysis (entanglement rate, cumulative valid rate, best-so-far progress) together support the central mechanism claim rather than just aggregate accuracy.

The paper is transparent about limitations (task-transfer failures on BFS/Floyd-Warshall/KMP, higher search-time cost from extra LLM calls, manually defined two-factor factorization), which increases trust in the reported results.
Search dynamics are analyzed at the process level (entanglement, executability, valid rate), providing mechanistic evidence for why factor-isolated edits help, rather than only end-task accuracy.
weaknesses: The headline '28.1x sample-efficient speedup' rests on questionable accounting: it compares 57 evaluated candidates from SPARK's own run against EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation setting, but the two methods operate under different protocols (EvoPrompting evolves per task; SPARK evolves only on dfs and transfers), and the EvoPrompting DFS number (68.14) is taken from the original paper rather than re-run in the authors' harness. This conflates protocol differences with method differences.

There is an LLM confound in baseline comparisons: EvoPrompting and EoH numbers derive from their original papers/settings with different (older) LLMs, while SPARK uses DeepSeek-R1-0528, a much stronger code model. The claimed gains over EP/EoH may substantially reflect model capability rather than the SPARK operator; only OE and FS are re-run under the same editor.

Statistical support for the main tables is thin. The main CLRS results (Tables 1 and 3) appear to come from single search runs of 100 attempts, and LLM-driven search is known to be high-variance; seed variance is only shown for one appendix figure (Fig. A.1). Without seed-level error bars in the main comparison, differences like 83.92 vs. 79.43 (EoH) are hard to interpret.

The method's scope is narrow: the OPERATOR/ACTION factorization is manually defined and tightly coupled to the CLRS program structure. On the five non-CLRS benchmarks, the factorization mechanism is not clearly instantiated (the factor definitions and feasibility constraints are described only for CLRS), and the gains there are small (20News +2pp, BCW +0.14, Mice tied), so the generalization claim beyond CLRS is weakly supported.

Several reported results raise interpretability concerns: e.g., Quickselect OOD accuracy remains ~10.7% in absolute terms, and some baselines score near zero, making relative framing potentially misleading; the FS/EoH non-CLRS rows use 400 candidates vs. 100 for SPARK/OE, complicating the comparison in Tables A.4/A.5.

Presentation: the paper over-relies on quoted branded phrases ('Searching: Function→Patch', 'Function-factor Tokens', 'Holistic edits', 'Predictable outcomes') repeated throughout, which adds verbosity without technical content; the code-availability URL appears truncated/missing, weakening reproducibility.

The contribution is largely prompt-orchestration and region-constrained decoding around an existing evolutionary backbone (OpenEvolve); the conceptual novelty over structure-aware mutation operators in classical NAS and over grammar/AST-constrained code generation is acknowledged but the delta is modest.

strengths: The controlled comparison design is a clear strength: SPARK is compared against OpenEvolve under an identical search backbone (OpenEvolve) and identical LLM editor (DeepSeek-R1-0528), which makes the contribution of the factor-scoped editing operator separable from the evolutionary infrastructure.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough: Table 3 decomposes ASR vs. RC+SAR across two LLM editors (DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus), and Table A.2 includes scope-control variants (region tags only, fixed-scope, random-scope) that help rule out the explanation that gains come merely from adding region tags.

The paper reports both a representative 10-task subset and the full 30-task CLRS comparison (Appendix A.1), addressing task-selection bias, and honestly discloses transfer failures (BFS, Floyd–Warshall, KMP) rather than hiding them.

Budget accounting is explicitly defined (proposal attempts vs. evaluated candidates, seed architecture counted), and the limitations section candidly identifies manual two-factor factorization, extra LLM call overhead, and non-uniform transfer as open issues.

The search-dynamics analysis (Fig. 2: entanglement rate, cumulative valid rate, best-so-far accuracy) provides mechanistic evidence linking the proposed mechanism to observed improvements, rather than reporting only endpoint numbers.
weaknesses: The core method is a relatively simple engineering contribution dressed in inflated terminology: 'Architecture Scope Router', 'Refinement Compass', and 'Scoped Architecture Refiner' are essentially three role-specific prompts, and the enforcement mechanism is region boundary tags plus a line-based diff check. The paper itself concedes that structure-aware/grammar-constrained editing is well established (Sec. 2), so the conceptual novelty beyond 'constrain the LLM to edit one of two labeled code regions' is limited.

The headline '28.1× sample-efficient speedup' claim is methodologically questionable. It compares SPARK's 57 evaluated candidates on DFS under a search-and-transfer protocol against EvoPrompting's best DFS result under a 1600-evaluation, per-task evolution protocol. These are different search regimes, different budgets, and different transfer settings; presenting the ratio as a like-for-like speedup overstates the contribution. The asymmetry is compounded by SPARK's feasibility pipeline rejecting non-executable proposals before they count toward the budget.

Baseline budgets are not comparable across methods in Table 1: OE and FunSearch are run at 100 attempts while EoH uses 400 and EvoPrompting effectively 1600 evaluations. Results at such heterogeneous budgets make the main-table ranking difficult to interpret.

Evidence of generality is weak. The factorization into OPERATOR/ACTION is manually defined for a single seed program's structure; on the five non-CLRS benchmarks, gains are mixed and often marginal (Mice Protein identical to OpenEvolve at 61.78, BCW +0.14, 20News +2.03), and it is unclear how the two-factor decomposition is instantiated on those tasks at all. The broad claims of cross-benchmark applicability are not well supported.

The full 30-task results reveal substantial regressions (BFS 99.7→70.6, FW 48.5→32.9, KMP 19.5→14.9) under the DFS-search-and-transfer protocol, indicating the method can overfit the search task; the paper mentions this but does not analyze why, and the aggregate mean masks these failures.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the main claims. Table 1 and the DFS headline number (83.74 reached at iteration 57) appear to come from limited runs; variance/seed reporting is only provided for the auxiliary dynamics analysis (Fig. A.1), and the main tables lack error bars or significance tests.

Reproducibility concerns: the abstract states 'Our code is available at' with no actual link provided, and several critical implementation details (exact region-tag definitions, the entanglement criterion, feasibility-check implementation, prompt templates) are deferred to an appendix that is not included in the manuscript. As submitted, the work cannot be reliably reproduced.

The theoretical justification for why entanglement hurts search (feasibility as p_v^k for k scopes) is informal and hand-wavy; it is presented as motivation rather than tested, and the entanglement metric is defined post hoc within SPARK's own region framework, which structurally favors SPARK in Fig. 2b.

The paper's framing that the bottleneck is 'not the absence of architectural knowledge' but edit controllability is asserted rather than established; no experiment directly isolates knowledge activation from, e.g., simply better prompt engineering or more LLM calls per proposal (SPARK uses 3+ LLM calls per attempt vs. 1 for baselines, a confound acknowledged only in limitations).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies 'functional entanglement' (a single edit coupling multiple interacting functional decisions) as a concrete, diagnosable failure mode of free-form LLM-driven NAS, and supports this with search-dynamics evidence (entanglement rate, cumulative valid rate, best-so-far progress in Fig. 2).

Methodologically careful controlled comparison: SPARK and the OpenEvolve baseline share the identical evolutionary backbone, LLM editor, prompt discipline, and attempt budget, so the reported deltas are attributable to the factor-scoped editing operator rather than infrastructure.

Substantive ablation evidence: Table 3 isolates ASR vs. RC+SAR under two different LLM editors (DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus) with consistent qualitative trends, and Appendix A.2 (Table A.2) further rules out the trivial explanation that region tags alone explain the gains (Random-Scope SAR reaches only 50.27 vs. 80.50 for full SPARK).

Honest and useful limitations section: the authors candidly report task-transfer failures (BFS, Floyd–Warshall, KMP degrade on the full 30-task suite, e.g., FW 48.5→32.9), the extra LLM-call overhead, and the manual two-factor design; the 30-task full-suite results in Table A.1 are reported to mitigate task-selection bias.

MACs accounting is used thoughtfully to show gains are not driven by capacity increases, and the evolution-trace analysis (Appendix A.6, Listings 1–6) makes the search behavior inspectable and interpretable.
weaknesses: The headline 28.1× 'sample-efficiency speedup' is built on an asymmetric budget comparison: 57 evaluated candidates for SPARK versus EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation setting, where EP also evolves across multiple tasks while SPARK searches only on dfs. The accounting conflates proposal attempts, evaluated candidates, and full training evaluations across methods with different protocols; a like-for-like efficiency claim (e.g., wall-clock or GPU-hours, which appear only in Table A.5) would be more defensible.

Table 1 does not state the number of seeds or variance for any method; given the known run-to-run volatility of LLM-driven evolutionary search (which the authors' own Fig. A.1 min–max bands show is substantial), single-point comparisons such as 83.92 vs. 79.43 (EoH) may not be statistically meaningful.

The central design—the two-factor decomposition into OPERATOR/ACTION with disjoint region tags—is hand-crafted for this specific CLRS program structure. Whether the claimed generality ('backbone-agnostic', transferable to other task interfaces) holds is only weakly tested: the five non-CLRS benchmarks appear to reuse the same high-level interface without explaining how factors are defined there, and Table 2 compares only against OpenEvolve in the main text.

The 'ASR only' and 'RC+SAR only' ablation variants (Table 3) are under-specified; ASR is a scope-selection module, so what exactly is edited when ASR runs without SAR/RC is unclear, weakening the causal interpretation of the ablation.

The theoretical motivation for why entanglement hurts (feasibility ≈ p_v^k for k scopes) is a trivial independence assumption and does not engage with the actual coupling structure between Operator and Action factors in the code.

Novelty is modest: factor-scoped constrained editing via region tags, deterministic parsing, and feasibility filters is close in spirit to existing structure-aware decoding and grammar/AST-constrained code generation and to mutation operators in classical NAS; the contribution is a well-executed NAS-specific instantiation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the abstract's code URL is truncated/empty, full prompt templates and the exact entanglement-rate criterion are deferred to an appendix without full detail in the reviewed pages, and it is unclear whether baseline numbers (EP/FS/EoH) in Table 1 are rerun under the identical budget or taken from prior work—the text implies mixed provenance, complicating comparison.
